title: Bulgarian — Streamlined System (Transliteration Act 2009; passports and ID documents)
authority: Transliteration Act (Закон за транслитерацията), State Gazette No. 19 of 13.03.2009, Arts. 4–6; Regulation for Issuing Bulgarian Personal Documents (ПМС 13 of 08.02.2010), Art. 2(1) and Appendix 1; UN resolution X/7 (2012); BGN/PCGN 2013
description: The statutory Bulgarian romanization (the 'Streamlined System'), mandatory for official use, geographical names and road signs, and used through Appendix 1 of the 2010 Regulation for names in passports and ID cards. Digraphs zh/ts/ch/sh/sht, Й→y, Х→h, Ъ→a, Ь→y, Ю→yu, Я→ya; word-final -ия → -ia (Мария → Maria, София → Sofia).
notes: Art. 5(1) letter combinations (дж→dzh, дз→dz, ьо→yo, йо→yo) give the same result as letter-by-letter mapping; they are listed as rules only to document the Act.

Art. 5(2) -ия → -ia applies only at the end of a word (end of string, space, hyphen: София-юг → Sofia-yug); inside a word ия stays iya (Илиян → Iliyan). The Act applies it to every word; Appendix 1 of the 2010 Regulation states it for personal names and settlement names, which is the same thing for names.
Art. 6: the name of the State България is romanized Bulgaria by tradition (not Balgaria); implemented as a whole-word rule. Derived words (български, българин) follow the table.

Regulation Art. 2(2): at the first identity document a citizen may request a different Latin spelling of 'characteristic letters and letter combinations' (e.g. Simeon Djankov, Ivan Stancioff). Such personal spellings cannot be predicted; generate variants for matching. Art. 2(3)–(6) govern later changes.
Art. 9: names from Latin-script languages keep their original spelling and names from other scripts follow that language's system; the scheme cannot detect such names.
Not reversible: ъ and а both give a; й and ь both give y; zh/sh/ts/sht also arise from з+х, с+х, т+с, ш+т (изход → izhod).

History: BDS 1596:1973 used й→j, ю→ju, я→ja, ц→c (see bg_bds_1596); the 1999 ID-document table changed Й/Ю/Я to Y/YU/YA; Bulgaria's 2012 UN paper says the 2009 Act changed Ц from C to TS, while Wikipedia says ts was introduced by a 2000 amendment. The -ia exception dates from 2006 (given and geographical names) and was extended to all word-final -ия in 2009. Older documents may show Cvetan, Mariya, Iordan (ICAO generic), Khristo (BGN/PCGN 1952), Jordan (BDS).

ICAO Doc 9303 §6.B generic Cyrillic values (Й→I, Х→KH, Ъ→IE, Ю→IU, Я→IA) conflict with Bulgarian law and are not used; only its Bulgarian exception Щ→SHT agrees. A Bulgarian MRZ is presumed to be the upper-case Appendix 1 string (inferred; no MRZ specimen checked).
Accented ѝ/ѐ map to i/e. Combining stress marks (U+0301, U+0300) are deleted by aliases before matching, so a stressed Мари́я still ends in -ия → Maria.

rules.note: Art. 6: the State name by established tradition
